Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

📅 20 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals.
  • What makes a good player great, and a great player the best?
  • After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals.

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Sources indicate that based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

It has been revealed that one lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

In a recent development, around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

Sources indicate that but the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Industry observers note that there is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

In a recent development, at the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s initiative was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

Why is 46-year-old Ronaldinho returning to soccer with Ravenna, an Italian third division club?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ronaldinho, one of the greatest footballers of all time, will be back on the pitch on Sunday, Nov.
  • "I'm really looking forward to this moment and coming back to Italy once more."@10Ronaldinho notes he can't wait to return to professional football with Ravenna at age 46 💪 pic.twitter.com/0UMdkhgFlY.
  • Ravenna, who have a history of playing in Italy's lower divisions, were acquired in 2024 by Ignazio Cipriani, the nephew of Arrigo Cipriani, the founder of the iconic Harry's Bar in Venice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ronaldinho, one of the greatest footballers of all time, will be back on the pitch on Sunday, Nov. 15, for a historic day. The Brazilian striker, who won the 2005 edition of the Ballon d'Or and played for PSG, Barcelona and AC Milan at the peak of his European career, signed a deal in the summer of 2026 to join the roster of Ravenna, an Italian team presently playing in the third division. Ronaldinho, who played his last professional match in 2015 and will turn 47 next year, is expected to play some minutes in the home derby against Forli, and you can watch it all on Paramount+. But let's break down how and why he's coming back to play after more than a decade and after announcing his retirement in 2018.

"I'm really looking forward to this moment and coming back to Italy once more."@10Ronaldinho notes he can't wait to return to professional football with Ravenna at age 46 💪 pic.twitter.com/0UMdkhgFlY.

Ravenna, who have a history of playing in Italy's lower divisions, were acquired in 2024 by Ignazio Cipriani, the nephew of Arrigo Cipriani, the founder of the iconic Harry's Bar in Venice. The Cipriani Group operates high-end restaurants, private members' clubs (Casa Cipriani), luxury hotels, event venues and branded residences across major international cities, such as New York City, London, Monaco, Miami and Dubai. Basically, it is now positioning itself as a global luxury lifestyle and real estate player, rather than simply a restaurant group.

"Today I do a lot of Footy Volley. I'm training differently."The legendary @10Ronaldinho talks coming out of retirement after 11 years to suit up for Ravenna in Serie C this weekend 👀 pic.twitter.com/z0cSOHd2k4.

Industry observers note that this is why Cipriani created links with some of the most notable figures in the world: soccer players, politicians, singers, actors and more. When the group entered the world of soccer, it brought in people who had already worked at the highest level of the game, such as former AC Milan sporting director Ariedo Braida, who played a key role alongside former AC Milan CEO Adriano Galliani in building AC Milan's legacy under Silvio Berlusconi's presidency. Braida left AC Milan in 2013 after 27 years.

Ravenna's current head coach is Andrea Mandorlini, who spent several years coaching in Serie A and represented Inter as a player between 1984 and 1991. The connection with Ronaldinho, who joined AC Milan in 2008 during Braida's tenure at the club, also involves another key figure at Ravenna: Lorenzo Tonetti, the club's head of external relations. During Ronaldinho's time at AC Milan, Tonetti owned Giannino, a restaurant in Milan that became something of a second home for several of the club's players. It was also a favorite meeting place for Galliani, who famously negotiated several transfer deals within its walls. Curiously, one of the waiters working there at the time was Giuseppe Riso, now one of the best-known agents in soccer, who represents players such as Sandro Tonali, Davide Frattesi and Carlos Augusto.

Sources indicate that ronaldinho signed a dual player-investor contract in the summer of 2026. He joined Ravenna with the ultimate aim of scoring one final professional goal while also acquiring an ownership stake in the club. Rather than having him play every week, his deal focuses on global marketing and special appearances in marquee matches, such as the local derby against Forli that will take place on Sunday. Ronaldinho is one of the most notable players in the history of the game. He joined Barcelona in 2003, where he became a global superstar, winning two FIFA World Player of the Year awards, the 2005 Ballon d'Or and the UEFA Champions League in 2006. In 2008, he moved to AC Milan, where he played until 2011. At the international level, he was a key part of Brazil's national team that won the 2002 World Cup. He formally retired in 2018 but played his last-ever football game three years earlier, in 2015.
